1.pericope_label: Elihu spake moreover, and said, Thinkest thou this to be right, that thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God’s? For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee? and, What profit shall I have, if I be cleansed from my sin? I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee. Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds which are higher than thou. If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man.

schools.summary: Ellicott judges this another misrepresentation of what Job had said, since Job did not mean that he was none the better for being righteous but only that his righteousness had not delivered him from suffering, and he observes that Elihu is here saying very much what Eliphaz and Bildad had said before; he then enters the chapter's sharpest caveat, that while it is indeed true God is too high to be affected by man's righteousness or unrighteousness, it does not follow that he is indifferent, for then he would not be a righteous judge. Delitzsch recasts the charge as one ponderous construction of co-ordinate questions, making the complaint one of non-requital rather than self-comparison.

Gill alone lets the whole charge stand, granting that Job had not said it in so many words but holding it fairly inferred from what he had said; he draws the distinction the complaint blurs, that a man's righteousness is of no advantage as to justification or title to happiness but of great advantage otherwise, and enters the qualification that because sin harms others God resents it and punishes for it even though it cannot harm him.

Clarke denies the charge outright, holding that my righteousness is more than God's would indeed be a blasphemous saying but that Job never said it either directly or constructively, and rendering the Hebrew instead I am righteous before God, a character Job had a right to assume because God himself had given it to him; on the argument from the heavens he takes their bare sight as enough to show God infinitely beyond us, derives the clouds from a root meaning to contend, and renders the conclusion literally, that to a man like thyself is thy wickedness and to the son of man thy righteousness, so that God can be neither hurt nor profited.

Henry is the one voice who thinks the first count substantially just, holding that when Job insisted so much on his integrity and on the severity of God's dealings he did in effect say it, as though on a balanced account God would be brought in debtor to him; but he refuses the second count, since Job had put the words about no profit in the mouth of prospering sinners and disclaimed them, and it is not a fair way of disputing to charge men with consequences they expressly renounce. He calls the malice of sinners impotent malice and sets against Job's reckoning the challenge no man can take up, who has first given to God.

debates: Whether Elihu quotes Job fairly, where Clarke denies that Job ever said it directly or constructively, Ellicott calls it another misrepresentation, Henry allows the first count while refusing the second, and Gill lets the whole charge stand as fairly inferred.

What the complaint actually was, which Delitzsch recasts as a charge of non-requital, that God makes no distinction between righteousness and sin and leaves the former unrewarded, rather than a comparison of Job's righteousness with God's.

Whether the premise that God is unaffected settles anything, which Ellicott grants as true but refuses as sufficient, since it would follow that God is indifferent and therefore not a righteous judge.
outliers: Clarke reads the clouds as the ethers of the Vulgate, from a root meaning to contend, the agitated and conflicting air and light whose motion produces both light and heat.

Henry turns the appeal to the heavens devotionally, that God made man erect and bade him look up, and where idolaters looked up and worshipped the hosts of heaven we must worship the Lord of those hosts.
themes: Thinkest thou this to be right, that thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God’s?
For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee? and, What profit shall I have, if I be cleansed from my sin?
I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee.
Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds which are higher than thou.
If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him?
If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand?
Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man.

9.pericope_label: By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty. But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night; Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven? There they cry, but none giveth answer, because of the pride of evil men. Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it.

schools.summary: Ellicott puts a different construction on the complaint, taking the argument to be that among men there may be oppression but not with an almighty and just judge, so that the right course is to wait; he lays out the alternative reading of the songs in the night, by which the giver of them is the selfish and luxurious oppressor who spends the night in feasting, grants it an intelligible meaning, doubts whether the proverbial sense is natural here, and leaves the choice to individual taste and judgment, noting that it partly turns on whether the question Where is God my Maker belongs to the cry of the oppressed or is Elihu's own, which he thinks the better view. Delitzsch renders the cry as a call for help by reason of the arm of the great.

Gill offers three senses of the vanity God will not hear, as a lie, as what is uttered rashly in a passionate and revengeful spirit, which he allows is too often the case of those who cry under oppression, and as empty prayers asking only for outward mercies.

Clarke repeats one clause like a refrain through these verses, that they bewail their calamities but do not sorrow for the cause of them and cry against their oppressors but call not upon God, and that this is why they have no relief; he keeps the devotional sense of the songs in the night while reporting four rival renderings from the Chaldee, the Greek, the Syriac and Arabic, and Coverdale, and presses the comparison with the beasts hard, citing the ox that knows his owner and the ass his master's crib and observing that quadrupeds, reptiles and fowls have more gratitude to their masters than man has to his God.

Henry states Job's complaint without softening, that the oppressed cry under the arm of the mighty and God does not appear to right them, which Job could not reconcile with the justice of God and his government, and asks on his behalf whether a righteous God can so slowly hear and so slowly see; his answer is that the fault lies in the cries, which are complaining and wailing cries, the cry of nature and passion rather than of grace, not cried unto God with the heart though they howled upon their beds. On the beasts he makes an argument rather than an exclamation, that the greatest excellency of reason is to make us capable of religion, so that those who only cry and never look up do no more than the brutes.

debates: Who gives songs in the night, which Ellicott leaves open between God and the luxurious oppressor who spends it in revelry, while Clarke keeps the devotional sense and reports four further renderings from the versions and Coverdale.
Whose words Where is God my Maker are, the cry of the oppressed or Elihu's own comment, which Ellicott thinks is better regarded as Elihu's and which he says partly decides the previous question.

What the unheard vanity is, which Gill divides into a lie, a rash and revengeful outburst, and prayer for outward mercies only, while Ellicott reports that some take the whole clause as still part of the sufferers' cry, so that it is they who say it is all in vain.
outliers: Clarke renders the opening not by reason of the multitude but from among the multitude, the oppressed clamouring because of the mighty.
Ellicott reads the comparison with the beasts the other way about, that the oppression is so severe its victims forget God can give songs in the night.
themes: By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty.
But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night;
Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven?
There they cry, but none giveth answer, because of the pride of evil men.
Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it.

14.pericope_label: Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him. But now, because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity: Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers dost not behold him to the received rendering, and on the fifteenth verse says outright that it is very obscure, offering his own rendering that what God's anger has visited upon Job is as nothing compared with his deserts and that God has not regarded the great abundance of his sin; he sets two further renderings beside it, notes that the word he translates arrogance is found nowhere else and appears to mean abundance or superfluity, and holds that the general bearing is apparent however rendered, that Job is encouraged in his murmurings because God has dealt too leniently with him. He then allows that Elihu's reproaches must have been some of the heaviest Job had to bear.

Gill narrows the complaint carefully, granting that God is invisible in his nature but insisting that Job had seen him in his works, trusted him as his salvation and held a full persuasion of the beatific vision, so that the saying can only be about not seeing God on a throne of judgment, hearing and trying his cause and acquitting him, which Job had often desired and despaired of ever seeing.

Clarke approaches the saying textually, noting that several manuscripts read thou shalt not see me and the Greek thou shalt not see us, the unpointed consonants admitting either him or us, and he prefers for the fifteenth verse but now, because he visiteth not in his anger, drawing from it the maxim that because vengeance is not speedily executed the hearts of the children of men are set in them to do iniquity; at the close he turns the charge of multiplying words without knowledge on the whole book, holding that it applies very strongly and generally not only to Job's three friends but to Elihu himself, the contest being frequently a strife of words.

Henry takes Job's saying doubly, as a complaint that he could not discern the drift and design of God's severe dealings and as a despair of ever seeing better days again, and glosses the mood by observing that as in prosperity we think our mountain will never be brought low, so in adversity we think our valley will never be filled, which is as absurd as to think the flowing tide will always flow or the ebbing tide always ebb; he reads the fifteenth verse as meaning that because Job did not trust God the affliction which came at first from love now has displeasure mixed with it, and declines to follow the three friends in condemning Job for a hypocrite, charging him only with speaking unadvisedly when his spirit was provoked.

debates: What Job meant by saying he should not see God, which Henry takes as both a failure to discern the design of his afflictions and a despair of better days, Gill confines strictly to not seeing God on a throne of judgment acquitting him, and Clarke and Ellicott treat as a question of text and rendering.

How the fifteenth verse should be rendered, where Ellicott calls it very obscure and canvasses three constructions while preferring his own, and Clarke prefers because he visiteth not in his anger, both arriving at the sense that the delay of judgment emboldens the murmurer.

Whether the charge of multiplying words without knowledge is well aimed, which Clarke turns on the whole book, applying it strongly to the three friends and to Elihu himself, while Henry defends Elihu and holds the reproof a mercy to Job.
outliers: Clarke holds that the delay of judgment is no proof that it shall not be executed, nor the deferring of mercy any proof that God has forgotten to be gracious.
Ellicott adds that happily the judgment was not to be long deferred, pointing forward to the voice from the whirlwind.
themes: Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him.
But now, because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity:
Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge.
